The Fashoda Incident ended with French forces withdrawing after several months of military stalemate with the British in Fashoda (now in South Sudan).
The Southern Cross Expedition, the first British venture of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, departed London.
The United States Navy battleship USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana, Cuba, killing more than 260 people and precipitating the Spanish–American War.
The United States captured Guam from Spain in a bloodless event during the Spanish–American War.
The Winton Motor Carriage Company, one of the first American car companies, sold its first unit.
US president William McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution, annexing Hawaii as a territory of the United States.
White supremacists seized power and massacred black Americans during the Wilmington massacre, the only instance of a municipal government being overthrown in United States history.
A Category 1 hurricane made landfall in Azua Province in the Dominican Republic, destroying three large schooners at Santo Domingo; only one crew member on the three vessels survived.
A. E. J. Collins scored 628 runs not out, the highest recorded score in cricket until being surpassed in 2016.
Antonio Luna, Commanding General of the Philippine Army, was assassinated in the midst of the Philippine–American War.
Cyclone Mahina struck Bathurst Bay, Queensland, killing more than 300 people in one of the deadliest natural disasters in Australian history.
During a storm, the crew of Lynmouth Lifeboat Station transported their 10-ton lifeboat 15 miles overland in order to rescue a damaged schooner.
FC Barcelona, one of the most successful clubs in Spanish football, was founded by Swiss football pioneer Joan Gamper.
Pearl Hart, one of the few female outlaws of the American Old West, committed one of the last recorded stagecoach robberies, about 30 miles southeast of Globe, Arizona.
Philippine–American War: A 60-man Filipino rearguard was defeated at the Battle of Tirad Pass, but delayed the American advance long enough to ensure President Emilio Aguinaldo's escape.
Philippine–American War: American forces defeated troops commanded by Philippine president Emilio Aguinaldo at the Battle of Marilao River.
Philippine–American War: Malolos, capital of the First Philippine Republic, was captured by American forces.
Second Boer War: In the Battle of Magersfontein, Boers defeated British forces trying to relieve the Siege of Kimberley.
The Philippine–American War began when an American soldier, under orders to keep insurgents away from his unit's encampment, fired on a Filipino soldier in Manila.
Thousand Days' War: Columbian Liberal rebels repelled a Conservative government attack at the Battle of Peralonso.
A Chinese immigrant in San Francisco fell ill with the bubonic plague in the first epidemic of the disease in the continental United States.
A dust explosion at a coal mine near Scofield, Utah, U.S., killed at least 200 miners.
American temperance activist Carrie Nation entered a saloon in Kiowa, Kansas, and destroyed its stock of alcoholic beverages with rocks.
Boxer Rebellion: Allied naval forces captured the Taku Forts from Qing China after a brief but bloody battle.
Boxer Rebellion: The Imperial Chinese Army began a 55-day siege of the Legation Quarter in Peking.
Datu Muhammad Salleh, leader of a series of major disturbances in North Borneo, was shot dead in Tambunan, but his followers did not give up for five more years.
FC Bayern Munich, Germany's most successful football club, was founded.
Giacomo Puccini's opera Tosca, based on the play La Tosca by French dramatist Victorien Sardou, premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome.
Italian anarchist Gaetano Bresci assassinated King Umberto I of Italy in Monza.
N'Djamena, now the capital of Chad, was founded as Fort-Lamy by French commander Émile Gentil.
Robert Anderson Van Wyck, mayor of New York City, broke ground for a new underground Rapid Transit Railroad that would link Manhattan and Brooklyn.
Second Boer War: A 10,000-strong column of soldiers led by Lord Kitchener broke a 13-day siege of a small garrison.
Second Boer War: British cavalry led by John French defeated Boer forces to end a 124-day siege of Kimberley in present-day South Africa.
Second Boer War: British troops made a third unsuccessful attempt to lift the siege of Ladysmith in the Battle of Vaal Krantz.
Second Boer War: The Siege of Mafeking in South Africa was lifted after 217 days, a decisive victory for the British against the Boers.
The German ocean liner SS Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse became the first ship to send a wireless telegraph message to an onshore receiver.

The Great Galveston hurricane, the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history, struck Galveston, Texas, with estimated winds of 135 miles per hour (215 km/h) at landfall, killing at least 6,000 people.
The Southern Cross Expedition led by Carsten Borchgrevink achieved a new Farthest South of 78° 50'S, making the first landing at the Great Ice Barrier.
The first copies of the children's novel The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum were printed.
The second of the German Naval Laws was passed, authorising the doubling in size of the Imperial German Navy.
A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck the Black Sea, the most powerful ever recorded in the area.
At the Royal Exhibition Building in Melbourne, the flag of Australia flew for the first time.
English writer Beatrix Potter privately published 250 copies of The Tale of Peter Rabbit after several publishers' rejections.
Gustav Mahler's Symphony No. 4 premiered in Munich.
Mozaffar ad-Din, Shah of Persia, granted exclusive rights to prospect for oil in the country to businessman William Knox D'Arcy.
On the fifth anniversary of the death of their founder, Swedish chemist and industrialist Alfred Nobel, the first Nobel Prizes were awarded in Stockholm.
Philippine–American War: Filipino guerrillas killed more than forty American soldiers in a surprise attack on the town of Balangiga on the island of Samar.
The Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers began an ultimately unsuccessful strike to reverse its declining fortunes and organize large numbers of new members.
The construction of the House with Chimaeras commenced in Kyiv.
The first great gusher of the Texas oil boom was discovered in the Spindletop oil field near Beaumont.
Theodore Roosevelt became President of the United States at age 42, the youngest person ever to do so, eight days after William McKinley was fatally wounded in Buffalo, New York.
U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation and once the world's largest producer of steel, was founded by financier J. P. Morgan.
U.S. president William McKinley was fatally shot by anarchist Leon Czolgosz at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, and died eight days later.

U.S. vice president Theodore Roosevelt first publicly used the phrase "speak softly and carry a big stick" at the Minnesota State Fair, describing his philosophy of negotiating peacefully while simultaneously threatening to use military force.
With Beijing occupied by foreign troops from the Eight-Nation Alliance, Qing China was forced to sign the Boxer Protocol, an unequal treaty that ended the Boxer Rebellion.
A group of Russian explorers led by Baron von Toll left their camp on Bennett Island and disappeared without a trace.
A spectator stand collapsed during a football match at Ibrox Park in Govan, Scotland, killing 25 supporters and injuring more than 500 others.
An expedition led by Peruvian explorer and farmer Agustín Lizárraga discovered the Incan city of Machu Picchu.
In a ceremony at Westminster Abbey, Edward VII and Alexandra were crowned King and Queen of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor and Empress of India.
In the most fatal recorded mountaineering accident, 199 of the 210 members of an Imperial Japanese Army unit perished in a blizzard on the Hakkōda Mountains.
The Antikythera mechanism, the oldest known surviving geared mechanism, was discovered among artifacts retrieved from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
The Discovery Expedition under Robert Falcon Scott attained a new Farthest South point in Antarctica.
The Dorchester Heights Monument, memorializing the siege of Boston during the American Revolutionary War, was dedicated.
The Hexham Abbey high-altar cross, amongst the most important works produced that year by the Keswick School of Industrial Art, was unveiled on Good Friday.
The Second Boer War came to an end with the signing of the Treaty of Vereeniging in Pretoria, South Africa.
The first science fiction film, titled A Trip to the Moon and based on From the Earth to the Moon by Jules Verne, was released in France.
The medieval St Mark's Campanile in Venice collapsed, also demolishing the Loggetta del Sansovino.
A blockade against Venezuela, caused by President Cipriano Castro's refusal to pay foreign debts, was lifted.
A rockslide buried part of the Canadian mining town of Frank under 110 million tonnes of rock, killing around 70 people.
Alfred Deakin became the second Australian prime minister, succeeding Edmund Barton, who left office to become a founding justice of the High Court of Australia.
Anti-Jewish riots broke out in Kishinev, the capital of Bessarabia Governorate, causing the death of nearly 50 Jews and focusing worldwide attention on the persecution of Jews in Russia.
Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union, a militant organisation campaigning for women's suffrage in the United Kingdom.
French cyclist Maurice Garin won the first edition of the Tour de France.
In one of the deadliest single-building fires in United States history, the Iroquois Theatre fire in Chicago killed more than 600 people.
Macedonian rebels in Kruševo established a republic, which existed for ten days before Ottoman forces destroyed the town.
SS Petriana struck a reef near Point Nepean, leading to Australia's first major oil spill and a debate over the White Australia policy.
Samuel Griffith became the first Chief Justice of Australia, while Edmund Barton and Richard O'Connor became the first Puisne Justices of the High Court of Australia.
Slava, the last of five Borodino-class battleships, was launched by the Imperial Russian Navy.
Storm Ulysses struck Ireland, felling thousands of trees and causing damage to up to a quarter of all houses in Dublin.
The Scottish National Antarctic Expedition anchored in the South Orkney Islands with the intention of establishing the first weather station in Antarctic territory.
Blackstone Library, the first branch of the Chicago Public Library system, was dedicated.
Chris Watson became the first prime minister of Australia from the Australian Labor Party.
France and the United Kingdom signed the Entente Cordiale, agreeing to a peaceful coexistence after centuries of intermittent conflict.
Himalia, Jupiter's largest irregular moon, was discovered by Charles Dillon Perrine at the Lick Observatory in California.
In the worst maritime disaster involving a Danish merchant ship, SS Norge ran aground on Hasselwood Rock and sank in the North Atlantic, resulting in more than 635 deaths.
Irish author James Joyce began a relationship with Nora Barnacle, and subsequently used the date to set the actions for his 1922 novel Ulysses, commemorated as Bloomsday.
Italian composer Giacomo Puccini's Madama Butterfly premiered at La Scala in Milan to poor reviews, forcing him to revise the opera.
Longacre Square in Midtown Manhattan was renamed Times Square after the New York Times building.
Pitching for the Boston Americans, Cy Young threw the first perfect game in modern professional baseball.
President Theodore Roosevelt announced the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, justifying the exercise of "international police power" by the U.S. in the Western Hemisphere.
Realizing that the Russification of Lithuania was not working, the Russian Empire lifted the 40-year-old ban on publications written in Lithuanian language using the Latin alphabet.
Russo-Japanese War: The Japanese battleships Hatsuse and Yashima sank after striking several mines off Port Arthur, China.
Scottish National Antarctic Expedition: Led by William Speirs Bruce, the Antarctic region of Coats Land was discovered by the Scotia.
The Marconi International Marine Communication Company specified CQD (audio featured) as the distress signal to be used by its operators.
The first underground segment of the New York City Subway opened, connecting New York City Hall with Harlem.
The most successful football club in Portugal, S.L. Benfica, was founded in Lisbon as Sport Lisboa.
About 1,500 Cretans, led by Eleftherios Venizelos, met at the village of Theriso to call for the island's unification with Greece, beginning the Theriso revolt.
An earthquake hit the Kangra Valley in India, killing at least 20,000 people and destroying 100,000 buildings.
Authorities of the British Raj partitioned the Bengal Presidency, separating the largely Muslim eastern areas from the largely Hindu western areas.
Despite being blind in one eye, ice hockey player Frank McGee set the record for most goals in a Stanley Cup game when he scored 14 against the Dawson City Nuggets.
First Russian Revolution: The crew of the Russian battleship Potemkin began a mutiny against their officers.
In a ceremony officiated by Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey, The Luck of Cumberland was presented to HMS Cumberland.
Nadir of American race relations: A mob of white Americans killed eight people in Oconee County, Georgia, as part of a mass lynching.
Sultan Abdul Hamid II established the Ullah millet, a separate millet for the Aromanians within the Ottoman Empire.
The 3,106-carat (621 g) Cullinan Diamond, the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found, was discovered at the Premier Mine in Gauteng, South Africa.
The Great Seimas of Vilnius met to discuss national concerns within Lithuania: they decided to demand wide political autonomy within the Russian Empire.
The Saint Petersburg Soviet held its first meeting, becoming the first elected body in Russia to represent workers.
Under the mediation of U.S. president Theodore Roosevelt, the Russo-Japanese War officially ended with the signing of a treaty at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Maine.
A deputation of Muslim leaders led by the Aga Khan III met Indian viceroy Lord Minto to secure greater political representation, eventually leading to the founding of the All-India Muslim League.
A team of Italian archaeologists led by Ernesto Schiaparelli discovered the tomb of Kha and Merit, an ancient Egyptian foreman and his wife, in the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina.
Alberto Santos-Dumont flew his biplane 14-bis for 50 metres (160 ft) at an altitude of about four metres (13 ft).
An earthquake registering approximately 8.2 Mw struck Valparaíso, Chile, killing 3,882 people.
Members of the U.S. Army's all-black 25th Infantry Regiment were accused of killing a white bartender and wounding a white police officer in Brownsville, Texas, despite exculpatory evidence.
Romanian inventor Traian Vuia became the first person to fly a heavier-than-air monoplane with an unassisted takeoff.

The All-India Muslim League, a political party in British India that developed into the driving force behind the creation of Pakistan as a Muslim state on the Indian subcontinent, was founded in Dhaka.
The Azusa Street Revival, the primary catalyst for the spread of Pentecostalism in the 20th century, opened in Los Angeles.
The Great Northern, Piccadilly and Brompton Railway, a 14.17 km long deep-level underground tube railway connecting Hammersmith and Finsbury Park, London, opened.
The Illinois Memorial, honoring Union army soldiers from Illinois who fought at the Siege of Vicksburg, was dedicated at Vicksburg National Military Park.
The Robert Burns Memorial Statue, the first public statue erected in New Brunswick, was dedicated in Fredericton.
The Royal Navy battleship HMS Dreadnought was launched, representing such a marked advance in naval technology that her name came to be associated with an entire generation of battleships.
The SS Valencia was wrecked off the coast of Vancouver Island, Canada, in a location so treacherous it was known as the Graveyard of the Pacific.
The ocean liner RMS Mauretania, the largest and fastest ship in the world at the time, was launched in Tyneside, England.
The second of two games between two Ohio football teams took place, after which accusations were made that players conspired to deliberately lose games.
Vauxhall Bridge in London opened, crossing the River Thames between Vauxhall and Westminster.
A mine explosion in Monongah, West Virginia, killed 362 people and led to the establishment of the United States Bureau of Mines.
An earthquake registering 6.2 Mw struck Kingston, Jamaica, resulting in approximately 1,000 deaths.
Charles Curtis of Kansas, a citizen of the Kaw Nation, became the first Native American U.S. Senator.
During the Brown Dog affair, protesters marched through London and clashed with police officers in Trafalgar Square over the existence of a memorial for animals that had been vivisected.
Gertrude Stein meets her life partner and muse, Alice B. Toklas in Paris.
Inspired by the Folies Bergère of Paris, American impresario Florenz Ziegfeld Jr. staged the first of his Ziegfeld Follies.
Italian educator Maria Montessori opened her first school and day-care centre for working-class children in Rome, employing a philosophy of education that now bears her name.
Japan and the United States signed a gentleman's agreement whereby the former would not permit further emigration to the U.S., while the latter would not limit Japanese immigration.
Minas Geraes, the first of three Brazilian dreadnought battleships, was laid down, sparking a vastly expensive South American naval arms race with Argentina and Chile.
More than 3,000 women in London participated in the Mud March, the first large procession organised by the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies.
New York City held its first annual ball drop event in Times Square as part of New Year's Eve celebrations.
Organized by Vladimir Lenin and Joseph Stalin, among others, Bolshevik revolutionaries robbed a bank stagecoach in Tiflis, present-day Georgia.
Pike Place Market, one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers' markets in the U.S. and a popular tourist attraction, opened in Seattle, Washington.
The British colony of New Zealand officially became a dominion to reflect its political independence since the 1850s.
The Workers' Federation of Chile declares a general strike in solidarity with an ongoing rail workers' strike.
The last confirmed sighting of the now-extinct huia occurred in the Tararua Range on New Zealand's North Island.
The original Parliament House in Wellington, New Zealand, was destroyed by fire.

American diplomat Durham Stevens, an employee of Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was fatally shot in San Francisco by two Korean immigrants unhappy with his support of increased Japanese presence in Korea.
An earthquake registering 7.1 Mw struck near Messina, which, along with the subsequent tsunami, killed at least 75,000 people in southern Italy.
As a result of numerous atrocities in the territory, the Congo Free State was annexed to Belgium to form the Belgian Congo.
Austria-Hungary announced the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, causing a crisis that permanently damaged the country's relations with the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Serbia.
Blücher, the last armored cruiser built by the Imperial German Navy, was launched.
British suffragette Margaret Travers Symons became the first woman to speak in the House of Commons when she escaped from her escort into the chamber and shouted at the assembly.
The first Hauser Dam in the U.S. state of Montana failed, causing severe flooding and damage downstream.
The first production Ford Model T, the car credited with initiating the mass use of automobiles in the United States, was completed at the Ford Piquette Avenue Plant in Detroit, Michigan.
A deed was recorded for David Hanbury to sell Island No. 2 in northern California to his brother John for $10.
A military coup against the government of Dimitrios Rallis began in the neighbourhood of Goudi in Athens, Greece.
Belgian chemist Leo Baekeland announced his invention of Bakelite, the world's first synthetic plastic.
British explorer Aeneas Mackintosh, a member of the Nimrod Expedition, escaped death by fleeing across ice floes.
Fifty-nine days after leaving New York City with three passengers, Alice Huyler Ramsey arrived in San Francisco to become the first woman to drive an automobile across the contiguous United States.
Following a reactionary military revolt against the Committee of Union and Progress, a mob began a massacre of Armenian Christians in the Adana Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire.
Pluto was photographed for the first time at the Yerkes Observatory in Williams Bay, Wisconsin, U.S., 21 years before it was officially discovered by Clyde Tombaugh.
The Manhattan Bridge, connecting Lower Manhattan to Downtown Brooklyn and considered to be the forerunner of modern suspension bridges, opened to traffic.
The Montreal Canadiens, the oldest professional ice hockey club in the world, were founded as a charter member of the National Hockey Association.
The ferry SS Penguin struck a rock in Wellington Harbour and sank, killing 75 people in New Zealand's worst maritime disaster of the 20th century.
The first Grey Cup, the championship game of the Canadian Football League, was held in Toronto.
The inaugural edition of the Giro d'Italia, a long-distance multiple-stage bicycle race, began in Milan; the Italian cyclist Luigi Ganna was the eventual winner.
The sixteen United States Navy battleships of the Great White Fleet, led by USS Connecticut, completed a circumnavigation of the globe.
Two men committed an armed robbery in Tottenham, London, and led police on a two-hour chase, partially by tram, that ended in the perpetrators' suicides.
A seventeen-month-long strike, which at its peak involved 15,000 coal miners represented by the United Mine Workers across 65 mines, began in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, U.S.
Aviator Eugene Burton Ely performed the first takeoff from a ship, flying from a makeshift deck on USS Birmingham in Hampton Roads, Virginia.
Construction was completed on the Buffalo Bill Dam, then the tallest dam in the world, on the Shoshone River in the U.S. state of Wyoming.
Freda Du Faur became the first woman to climb Aoraki / Mount Cook, the highest peak in New Zealand.
French aviator Raymonde de Laroche became the first woman to receive a pilot's licence.
Frenchman Louis Paulhan landed his biplane at Manchester, having departed from London the previous day, to win the world's first long-distance air race.
Glacier National Park was established in the U.S. state of Montana.
Gustav Mahler's Symphony No. 8, one of the largest-scale choral works in the classical concert repertoire and popularly known as the "Symphony of a Thousand", was first performed in Munich.
HMS Niobe arrived in Halifax Harbour to become the first large ship of the Royal Canadian Navy.

Hurricane-force winds combined hundreds of small fires in the U.S. states of Washington and Idaho into the Devil's Broom fire, which burned about 4,700 square miles (12,100 km²), the largest fire in recorded U.S. history.
Old Trafford, a football stadium in Greater Manchester, England, hosted its inaugural match, between Manchester United and Liverpool.
Parliament passed the People's Budget, the first budget in British history with the express intent of redistributing wealth.

Prospectors drilled into a pressurized deposit within the Midway-Sunset Oil Field in California, resulting in the largest accidental oil spill in history, which eventually released 9 million barrels (9 e6oilbbl) of crude oil over 18 months.
SMS Zrínyi, one of the last pre-dreadnoughts built by the Austro-Hungarian Navy, was launched in Trieste.
Six English towns amalgamated to form a single county borough called Stoke-on-Trent, the first union of its type.
The United States Congress passed the Mann Act, which prohibited the interstate transport of females for "immoral purposes".
The crews of three Brazilian warships – all commissioned only months before – and several smaller vessels mutinied against perceived "slavery" being practised in the Brazilian Navy.
William D. Boyce established the Boy Scouts of America, expanding the Scout Movement into the United States.
A gun battle in the East End of London left two dead and sparked a political row over the operational involvement of Winston Churchill, then Home Secretary.
A mine explosion near Briceville, Tennessee, killed 84 miners despite a well-organized rescue effort led by the United States Bureau of Mines.
American cartoonist Winsor McCay released the silent short film Little Nemo (featured), one of the earliest animated films.
An earthquake registering 7.7 Mw destroyed Almaty in Russian Turkestan.
An explosion of badly degraded propellant charges on board the French battleship Liberté detonated the forward ammunition magazines and destroyed the ship.
Calbraith Perry Rodgers completed the first transcontinental flight across the United States.
Construction began on the Saline Valley salt tram, which during its operation was the steepest tram in the United States.
Edith Maryon's statuette The Dance of Anitra, one of the few of her works known to survive in private hands, was exhibited at the Royal Academy of Arts.
English dramatist W. S. Gilbert of the songwriting duo Gilbert and Sullivan died while saving a young woman from drowning in his lake.
Established by Clara Zetkin, Käte Duncker, and others, International Women's Day was first observed.
Four countries signed the North Pacific Fur Seal Convention, which banned the hunting of seals in the pelagic zone.
Harriet Quimby became the first woman to earn an Aero Club of America aviator certificate.
His Majesty's Airship No. 1, Britain's first rigid airship, was wrecked by strong winds before her maiden flight at Barrow-in-Furness.
In a case later termed a "legal lynching", Will P. Brady obtained a guilty verdict and death sentence against 15-year-old León Martínez Jr., five days after his arrest for killing a white woman.
King George V and Queen Mary were crowned at Westminster Abbey in London.
Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre by museum employee Vincenzo Peruggia and was not recovered until two years later.
Mexican Revolution: A force of Maderistas captured Torreón and proceeded to massacre 303 of the city's Chinese residents.
Mexican Revolution: The Magonista rebellion began when Mexican Liberal Party troops captured the town of Mexicali.

Mexican president Porfirio Díaz and the revolutionary Francisco I. Madero signed the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez to end hostilities between each other's forces, concluding the initial phase of the Mexican Revolution.
Moscow's Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception was consecrated.
Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and his team became the first people to reach the South Pole.
Prince Arthur, a son of Queen Victoria, became the first Governor General of Canada of royal descent, as well as the first Prince of Great Britain and Ireland to hold that position.
The Australasian Antarctic Expedition began with the departure of SY Aurora from London.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics conducted the first national census of the country.
The Corozal, the most powerful dredger built to that time, was launched in London for service in construction of the Panama Canal.
The Nakhla meteorite, the first meteorite to suggest signs of aqueous processes on Mars, fell to Earth in Abu Hummus, Egypt.
The Second Canton Uprising took place but was suppressed in Guangzhou, China.
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York City killed 146 sweatshop workers, many of whom could not escape because the doors to the stairwells and exits had been locked.
The Uruguayan Regional Workers' Federation declared a general strike in solidarity with trolley workers in Montevideo.
The Xinhai Revolution began with the Wuchang Uprising, marking the beginning of the collapse of the Qing dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China.
The last member of the Yahi, known as Ishi, emerged from the wilderness near Oroville, California, to join European American society.
American pilot Harriet Quimby became the first woman to fly across the English Channel.
Arthur Rose Eldred became the first person to attain the rank of Eagle Scout in the Boy Scouts of America.
At the All-Albanian Congress, the Assembly of Vlorë was constituted, which declared the independence of the Albanian Vilayet from the Ottoman Empire.
During a match, baseball star Ty Cobb enters the stands and assaults a fan who had heckled him, leading to his suspension.
Eight months after perishing during the ill-fated Terra Nova Expedition, the bodies of Robert Falcon Scott and his companions were discovered on the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica.
Following a reduction in pay, textile workers in Little Falls, New York, walked out of their mill, starting a three-month strike.
German geophysicist Alfred Wegener presented his theory of continental drift, the precursor of plate tectonics, to the German Geological Society.
Immigrant textile workers in Lawrence, Massachusetts, went on strike in response to a pay cut corresponding to a new state law shortening the working week.
More than 1,500 people on the Titanic died when the passenger liner sank after colliding with an iceberg southeast of Newfoundland.
Robert Falcon Scott's ill-fated Terra Nova Expedition reached the South Pole, only to find that Roald Amundsen's team had beaten them by 33 days.
Sultan Abd al-Hafid signed the Treaty of Fes, making Morocco a French protectorate.
The Albanian revolt ended when the Ottoman government agreed to meet most of the rebels' demands.
The Nefertiti Bust, listed among the "Top 10 Plundered Artifacts" by Time, was found in Amarna, Egypt, before being taken to Germany.
The keel of USS Nevada was laid down, beginning construction on the United States Navy's first "super-dreadnought".
The largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century began, forming the volcano Novarupta in the Alaska Peninsula.
A meteor procession was observed along a great circle arc from Canada to Brazil, leading astronomers to conclude that its source was a small, short-lived natural satellite of the Earth.
A rail workers' strike in Chile escalates into a general strike, organized by the Regional Workers' Federation of Chile.
A severe blizzard reached its maximum intensity in the Great Lakes Basin of North America, destroying 19 ships and 68,300 tons of cargo, and killing more than 250 people.
An agricultural workers' strike in Wheatland degenerated into a riot, becoming one of the first major farm-labor confrontations in California.
Arnold Schoenberg conducted the Vienna Concert Society in a concert of expressionist music that so shocked the audience that they began to riot.
At a ceremony at Kurrajong Hill, Lady Denman, wife of the governor-general Lord Denman, announced that the future capital of Australia would be called Canberra.
Carrying a cargo hold full of highly flammable chemicals, the ocean liner SS Volturno caught fire in the north Atlantic and sank, resulting in 136 deaths.
Cecil B. DeMille started filming Hollywood's first feature film, The Squaw Man (featured).
Claudio Monteverdi's last opera, L'incoronazione di Poppea, was performed theatrically for the first time in more than 250 years.
During a labor strike in Ipswich, Massachusetts, police opened fire into a crowd of strikers, killing one and injuring several others.

During the premiere of the ballet Le Sacre du printemps by Igor Stravinsky at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, the avant-garde nature of the music and choreography caused a near-riot in the audience.
Emily Davison, an activist for women's suffrage in the United Kingdom, was fatally injured after being trampled by a horse owned by King George V at the Epsom Derby.
First Balkan War: After a five-month siege, Bulgarian and Serbian forces captured the Ottoman city of Adrianople.
First Balkan War: The Greek army captured Bizani Fortress, near Ioannina, from the Ottomans.
Greek military aviators Michael Moutoussis and Aristeidis Moraitinis performed the first naval air mission in history, with a Farman MF.7 hydroplane.
Haruna, the fourth and last Japanese battlecruiser of the Kongō class, was launched and went on to serve in both world wars.
In Detroit, autoworkers for car manufacturer Studebaker went on strike in the American auto industry's first major strike action.
More than 360 were killed and 20,000 homes were destroyed in the Great Dayton Flood in Dayton, Ohio, U.S.
More than 50,000 Union and Confederate veterans gathered at the Gettysburg Battlefield, the largest combined reunion of American Civil War veterans ever held.
New York City's Grand Central Terminal, the world's largest train station by number of platforms, opened immediately after midnight.

Phan Xích Long, the self-proclaimed emperor of Vietnam, was arrested for organising a revolt against the colonial rule of French Indochina, which was nevertheless carried out by his supporters the following day.
Princess Victoria Louise of Prussia married Prince Ernest Augustus of Hanover; the occasion was one of the last great social events of European royalty before World War I began.
Public-transportation workers in Indianapolis went on strike, shutting down mass transit in the city.
Raja Harishchandra, the first Indian feature-length film, was released.
Second Balkan War: The Serbian Army began the Siege of Vidin, which they abandoned six days later when an armistice between the Serbs and Bulgarians was signed.
Seventy-three people were crushed to death in a stampede after someone falsely yelled "fire" at a crowded Christmas party in Calumet, Michigan, U.S.
The Armory Show, the first large modern-art exhibition in the United States, opened at the 69th Regiment Armory in New York City.
The Jew's Christmas, the first American film to include a rabbi as a character, was released.
The Russian inventor Igor Sikorsky flew the self-designed Russky Vityaz, the world's first four-engine fixed-wing aircraft.
The Shubert Theatre opened on Broadway with a production of Hamlet.
The United Mine Workers of America began a strike against the Rockefeller-owned Colorado Fuel & Iron Company, sparking the Colorado Coalfield War.
The Woolworth Building in New York City officially opened; at the time, it was the tallest building in the world, with a height of 792 feet.
The air temperature in Furnace Creek, California, reached 134 °F (56.7 °C), recognized by the World Meteorological Organization as the highest recorded on Earth.

The cricket pavilion at the Nevill Ground was destroyed in an arson attack that was attributed to militant suffragettes as part of a country-wide campaign co-ordinated by the Women's Social and Political Union.
The worst mining accident in the United Kingdom's history took place when an explosion resulted in 440 deaths at the Universal Colliery in Senghenydd, Wales.
Thousands of women marched in Washington, D.C., "in a spirit of protest" against the exclusion of women from American society.
While on a campaign in Bulgaria, the Romanian Army suffered a cholera outbreak that led to around 1,600 deaths.
A fire and a gun battle between the Colorado National Guard and striking coal miners led to 17 deaths in the Ludlow Massacre.
A large internal explosion destroyed HMS Bulwark near Sheerness, killing 741 people on board.
Andrew Fisher, who in his previous term as premier oversaw a period of reform unmatched in the Commonwealth until the 1940s, became Prime Minister of Australia for the third time.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Yugoslav nationalist, sparking the outbreak of World War I.
Around 2,000 members of European society attended a ball at Kenwood House, England, in one of the last major social events before the outbreak of the First World War.
As part of the Ottoman Empire's policies of ethnic cleansing, Turkish irregulars began a six-day massacre in the predominantly Greek town of Phocaea.
Due to price increases on macaroni products, rioting occurred in the Little Italy area of Providence, Rhode Island.
First World War: A squadron of the 4th Royal Irish Dragoon Guards attacked a German scout party, the first engagement of British forces on the Western Front.
First World War: Allied forces began engaging German troops at the First Battle of Ypres.
First World War: German forces captured Rossignol in Belgium, taking more than 3,800 French prisoners.
First World War: The Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force invaded German New Guinea, winning the Battle of Bita Paka.
First World War: The German submarine U-9 sank three Royal Navy cruisers, resulting in approximately 1,450 deaths.
First World War: The Imperial German Navy attacked ports in northern England, resulting in hundreds of civilian casualties.
George V reviewed more than 200 Royal Navy vessels at Spithead, England.
HMAS AE1, the Royal Australian Navy's first submarine, was lost at sea; its wreck was not found until 2017.
In the aftermath of the Balkan Wars, Greeks living in southern Albania proclaimed the short-lived Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus.
In their first major action of the First World War, the British Expeditionary Force engaged German troops in Mons, Belgium.
Japan captured Pohnpei from Germany, eventually leading to large-scale Japanese immigration to Micronesia.
Kid Auto Races at Venice, featuring the first appearance of comedy actor Charlie Chaplins character the Tramp, was released.
Off the coast of the Dutch island of Texel, a British naval squadron sank the German 7th Half Flotilla of torpedo boats in the Battle off Texel.
RMS Aquitania, the last surviving four-funnel ocean liner, departed from Liverpool on her maiden voyage to New York City.
RMS Britannic, the third and largest Olympic-class ocean liner of the White Star Line after RMS Olympic and RMS Titanic, was launched at the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast.
Seven-year-old Theo Faiss, later memorialized in speeches by Rudolf Steiner and a sculpture by Edith Maryon, was killed by an overturned wagon in Switzerland.
The Battle of Cer ended with the first Allied victory of World War I.
The Battle of Mulhouse began with France's first attack of World War I in an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to recover the region of Alsace from Germany.
The Cape Cod Canal, connecting Cape Cod Bay and Buzzards Bay in the U.S. state of Massachusetts, opened on a limited basis.
The Endurance departed Plymouth, England, on the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition.
The Franck–Hertz experiment, the first electrical measurement to clearly demonstrate quantum mechanics, was presented to the German Physical Society.
The French army's general headquarters was activated in anticipation of war with Germany.
The Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition began in an attempt to make the first land crossing of Antarctica.
The Karluk, the flagship of the Canadian Arctic Expedition, sank after being crushed by ice.
The Royal Navy armed trawler Night Hawk sank after striking a mine, with the loss of six of her crew.
The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line in the U.S. state of Florida became the first scheduled airline using a winged aircraft.
The US Navy launched the USS Nevada as its first Standard-type battleship.
The animated film Gertie the Dinosaur was released, later greatly influencing future animators such as the Fleischer brothers and Walt Disney.
The first shots of World War I were fired by the Austro-Hungarian river monitor Bodrog on Serbian defences near Belgrade.
The passenger pigeon, which once numbered in the billions, became extinct when the last individual died in captivity.
Under the Protocol of Corfu, the Principality of Albania officially recognized Northern Epirus as an autonomous self-governing region.
World War I: Adhering to the terms of the Treaty of London, the United Kingdom declared war on Germany in response to the latter's invasion of Belgium.

World War I: As the British Expeditionary Force and French Fifth Army began their retreat from Mons, the British II Corps delayed the pursuing Germans at the Battle of Le Cateau long enough for the main force to escape.
World War I: Austro-Hungarian forces launched an assault against Serbian defensive positions at the Kolubara river, beginning the Battle of Kolubara.
World War I: Belgian troops won a victory at the Battle of Halen, but were ultimately unable to stop the German invasion of Belgium.
World War I: British and German soldiers interrupted fighting to celebrate Christmas, beginning the Christmas truce.
World War I: During the sack of Louvain in Belgium, German troops burned the town's Catholic university, destroying hundreds of medieval manuscripts.
World War I: German naval forces bombarded Papeete in French Polynesia and sank a French gunboat.

World War I: Ignoring orders to retreat, Hermann von François led a successful counterattack defending East Prussia at the Battle of Stallupönen and scored the first German victory in the Eastern Front.
World War I: Off the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, the Australian light cruiser HMAS Sydney sank SMS Emden, the last active German warship in the Indian Ocean, at the Battle of Cocos.
World War I: The Battle of Tannenberg resulted in the almost complete destruction of the Russian 2nd Army by the German 8th Army.
World War I: The French army repulsed a German assault against their positions on high ground near the city of Nancy.
World War I: The German colony of Togoland surrendered to French and British forces after a 20-day campaign.
World War I: The Royal Navy dreadnought HMS Audacious was sunk by a mine, but its loss was kept secret for four years.
World War I: The civilian authorities of Antwerp surrendered and allowed the German army to capture the city.
World War I: The first contingent of the First Australian Imperial Force departed Albany, Western Australia.
Zaian War: Zaian Berber tribesmen routed French forces at the Battle of El Herri in Morocco.
A category 4 hurricane made landfall in Galveston, Texas, leaving at least 275 people dead.
About 30,000 people were killed when an earthquake struck the Province of L'Aquila in Italy.
California's Lassen Peak violently erupted, the only volcanic eruption in the contiguous U.S. in the 20th century until Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980.
First World War: Australian and New Zealand troops repelled the third attack on Anzac Cove, inflicting heavy casualties on the attacking Ottoman forces.
First World War: Britain, France and Russia signed a secret treaty promising territory to Italy if it joined the war on their side.
First World War: In one of the largest naval battles of the Gallipoli campaign, Ottoman forces sank three Allied battleships and severely damaged three others.

First World War: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Anzac Cove while British and French troops landed at Cape Helles to begin the Allied invasion of the Gallipoli peninsula in the Ottoman Empire.
First World War: The British and French prime ministers, H. H. Asquith and René Viviani, met at Calais to discuss future offensives including the Gallipoli campaign.
First World War: The French parliament passed a law granting the land occupied by British war graves as "the free gift of the French people".
Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition: SY Aurora, anchored in McMurdo Sound, broke loose during a gale, beginning a 312-day ordeal in the Ross Sea and Southern Ocean for her 18-man crew.
Japanese prime minister Ōkuma Shigenobu issued the Twenty-One Demands to China in a bid to increase Japan's power in East Asia.
Rebels led by John Chilembwe attacked local plantation owners, beginning an uprising regarded as a key moment in the history of Malawi.
Russia withdraws from its occupation of northwestern Iran, enabling a subsequent Ottoman invasion and massacres of Assyrians and Armenians.
Sepoys of Indian Muslim background mutinied against their British officers in Singapore.
The Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire began with the arrest and deportation of hundreds of prominent Armenians in Constantinople.
The Battle of Neuve Chapelle, the first deliberately planned British offensive of the First World War, began.
The Casablanca Fair opened in the French protectorate in Morocco.
The Zimmerwald Conference, the first of three international socialist conferences forming the Zimmerwald movement, opened in Switzerland.
The appointment of Mehmed Reshid as governor of Diyarbekir, Turkey, intensified the genocide of Syriac Christians by pro-Ottoman forces.
The oldest Royal Air Force station in continuous operation, RAF Northolt, opened as home to No. 4 Reserve Aeroplane Squadron.
U.S. Marines landed at Port-au-Prince to begin a nineteen-year occupation of Haiti.
World War I: British forces launched the Battle of Aubers, an offensive on the Western Front, as part of the larger Second Battle of Artois.
World War I: Hit by ground fire, French aviation pioneer Roland Garros landed his aircraft behind enemy lines and was taken prisoner by German forces.
World War I: Senior British and French figures, including prime ministers H. H. Asquith and Aristide Briand, met at Calais to discuss the future of the Salonika Front.
World War I: The first major attack of the German bombing campaign against Britain took place when Zeppelins bombed several towns in Norfolk.
A confrontation at Blargies prison camp in France led to a charge of mutiny for New Zealand private John Braithwaite, for which he was later executed.
An armed confrontation in Everett, Washington, between local authorities and members of the Industrial Workers of the World resulted in seven deaths.
An explosion, blamed on Austro-Hungarian saboteurs, sank the Italian dreadnought Leonardo da Vinci.
Congress passed the Philippine Autonomy Act, the first formal and official declaration of the U.S.'s commitment to grant independence to the Philippines.
First World War: Allied forces gained a strategic victory at the Battle of Magdhaba on the Sinai Peninsula.
First World War: Around 55,000 workers in Berlin went on strike to protest against the trial of anti-war campaigner Karl Liebknecht.
First World War: British mariner Charles Fryatt was executed in Bruges, Belgium, after a German court-martial found him guilty of being a franc-tireur.
First World War: Russian troops won a victory in the Battle of Kostiuchnówka, with the Polish Legions playing a key role on the Austro-Hungarian side.
First World War: Second Lieutenant Kléber Dupuy defeated a German attack on Fort Souville at a key moment of the Battle of Verdun.
First World War: The "worst 24 hours in Australia's entire history" occurred when Australian forces unsuccessfully attacked German defences at Fromelles, France.
First World War: The British Empire's Sinai and Palestine campaign began with a victory at the Battle of Romani.

First World War: The first day of the Battle of Albert, the opening phase of the Battle of the Somme, became the bloodiest day in the British Army's history, with 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 deaths.
Georgia Tech defeated Cumberland University 222–0 in the most lopsided college football game in American history.
Hussein, King of Hejaz, orchestrated a revolt against the Ottoman Empire with the aim of creating a single unified and independent Arab state.
In the congressional elections, Jeannette Rankin became the first woman elected to the United States House of Representatives.
Irish republicans led by Patrick Pearse began the Easter Rising against British rule in Ireland, and proclaimed the Irish Republic an independent state.
Jesse Washington, a teenage African-American farmhand, was lynched in Waco, Texas.
Lij Iyasu, the emperor-designate of Ethiopia, was deposed in favor of his aunt Zewditu.
Margaret Sanger established the United States' first family planning clinic in Brooklyn, New York.
Max Reger's Hebbel Requiem was first performed in a memorial concert for the composer, conducted by Philipp Wolfrum.
Oswald Boelcke and Max Immelmann became the first German aviators to be awarded the Pour le Mérite, Germany's highest military honour.
Six days after Pancho Villa and his cross-border raiders attacked Columbus, New Mexico, U.S. general John J. Pershing led a punitive expedition into Mexico to pursue him.

The final letter in the McMahon–Hussein Correspondence was written, agreeing that Britain would recognise Arab independence in return for the Sharif of Mecca launching a revolt against the Ottoman Empire.
The first Feminist Congress of Yucatán began in Mérida, Mexico, to propose reforms for women's social, educational, and legal rights.
The first issue of Irish War News was published in Ireland.
The first self-service grocery store, Piggly Wiggly, was founded in Memphis, Tennessee, U.S.
The province of Manitoba passed a law that first granted some Canadian women the right to vote.
Up to 1,000 lumber workers initiated a labor strike against the Virginia and Rainy Lake Lumber Company in Minnesota, United States, which lasted over a month.

World War I: Britain, France and Russia made the Declaration of Sainte-Adresse, stating that they would refuse to sign any peace treaty with the Central Powers that failed to ensure the political and economic independence of Belgium.
World War I: German agents sabotaged U.S.-made munitions in New York Harbor that were to be supplied to the Allies.
World War I: The Battle of Mont Sorrel in the Ypres Salient came to an end as a Canadian assault led German forces to withdraw to their original lines.
World War I: The Supreme War Command was established to oversee the armed forces of all the Central Powers.
A ship carrying TNT and picric acid in Halifax Harbour, Canada, caught fire after a collision and caused one of the largest accidental explosions in history.
A socialist convention in Leeds, United Kingdom, called for an end to the First World War and the establishment of Workers' and Soldiers' Delegates across the country.
Alexander was crowned King of Greece, succeeding his father Constantine I, who had abdicated.
At least 30,000 people witnessed the Miracle of the Sun in the fields of Cova da Iria near Fátima, Portugal.

Being unable to resolve disputes with Eddie Livingstone, owner of the Toronto Blueshirts, the other ice hockey clubs of Canada's National Hockey Association officially agreed to break away and form the National Hockey League.
First World War: Attempting to advance into Palestine, the British were defeated by Ottoman troops at the First Battle of Gaza.
First World War: Canadian forces captured Passendale, Belgium, after three months of fighting against the Germans at the Battle of Passchendaele.
First World War: Hussein al-Husayni, the Ottoman mayor of Jerusalem, surrendered the city to British forces.
First World War: New Zealand troops suffered more than 2,000 casualties, including more than 800 deaths, in the First Battle of Passchendaele, making it the nation's largest loss of life in one day.
First World War: The Allies devastated the German defence at the Battle of Broodseinde, prompting a crisis among German commanders and causing a severe loss of morale in the 4th Army.
First World War: The Battle of Cambrai began with British forces having initial success over Germany's Hindenburg Line.
First World War: The Battle of Passchendaele began near Ypres, Belgium, with the Allies aiming to force German troops to withdraw from the Channel Ports.
First World War: The British Army detonated 19 ammonal mines under German lines, killing perhaps 10,000 in the deadliest non-nuclear man-made explosion in history during the Battle of Messines.
First World War: The Canadian Corps began the first wave of attacks of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in Vimy, France.
First World War: Troops of the British Empire defeated Ottoman forces at the Battle of Rafa on the Sinai–Palestine border.
Following the overthrow of the Russian tsar Nicholas II, Georgia's bishops unilaterally restored the autocephaly of the Georgian Orthodox Church.
Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition: Seven survivors of the Ross Sea party were rescued after being stranded for several months.
In New York City, the NAACP and church and community leaders organized a silent march of at least 8,000 people to protest violence directed towards African Americans.
Mexican football club Toluca FC was founded by a group of local businessmen and sports enthusiasts.
Pope Benedict XV promulgated the Pio-Benedictine Code, the first official comprehensive codification of Latin canon law.
Russia and France reached an agreement to support one another's territorial ambitions for Europe in the aftermath of World War I.
Russian Revolution: Tsar Nicholas II was forced to abdicate in the February Revolution, ending three centuries of Romanov rule.
Serbian prime minister Nikola Pašić and Yugoslav Committee president Ante Trumbić signed the Corfu Declaration, agreeing to seek the establishment of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.
Serving as a British armed merchant cruiser, Laurentic was sunk by German naval mines off the northern coast of Ireland, resulting in 354 deaths.
The British government issued the Balfour Declaration in support of a Jewish homeland in Palestine, then an Ottoman region with a small Jewish minority.
The Broadhurst Theatre opened in New York City with a performance of Misalliance by George Bernard Shaw.
The Imperial War Graves Commission was established by royal charter to mark, record and maintain the graves and places of commemoration of British Empire military forces.
The Original Dixieland Jass Band recorded "Livery Stable Blues", the first jazz single ever released.
World War I: A delayed action bomb left by German troops exploded in the town hall of Bapaume, France, killing 24 soldiers and civilians.
World War I: A meeting of the German Crown Council decided upon the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare.
World War I: Allied forces defeated Turkish troops in Beersheba in Southern Palestine at the Battle of Beersheba, with the battle involving one of the last successful cavalry charges.
World War I: British forces captured Gaza following the retreat of the Ottoman garrison.
World War I: German naval officer Wilhelm Werner murdered 19 captured crew members of the British cargo ship SS Torrington by submerging when they were on deck.
World War I: German troops invaded Portuguese East Africa in an attempt to escape superior British forces to the north and resupply from captured Portuguese materiel.
World War I: Hugh Grosvenor, 2nd Duke of Westminster led a force to rescue 92 prisoners of war from Bir Hakeim, killing the Senussi guards and their families.
World War I: Several French army corps began a massive assault against the German-occupied Chemin des Dames ridge, south of Laon, France.
World War I: The Battle of Polygon Wood, part of the Battle of Passchendaele, began near Ypres, Belgium.
World War I: USS Jacob Jones became the first American destroyer to be sunk by enemy action when it was torpedoed by German submarine SM U-53.
A case of influenza was recorded at Camp Funston, Kansas, United States, conventionally marking the beginning of the Spanish flu pandemic.
A group of Red Guards hung a red lantern atop the tower of the Helsinki Workers' House, symbolically marking the start of the Finnish Civil War.
About 1,000 demonstrators marched on Government House in Darwin, Australia, where they burned an effigy of Administrator John Gilruth and demanded his resignation.
An explosion in the ammunition magazine of the Japanese battleship Kawachi resulted in the deaths of more than 600 officers and crewmen.
An underground explosion at a coal mine in Staffordshire, England, killed 155 men and boys.
At the general election in Ireland, Constance Markievicz was elected to the House of Commons of the United Kingdom as the first female member of Parliament, although she never took her seat.
Conscientious objector Henry Firth died in a work camp on Dartmoor, England, triggering a strike over living conditions.
Finnish Civil War: The Battle of Tampere started, leading to the capture of approximately 11,000 Red prisoners, and turning the tide of the war in favour of the Whites.
First World War: British and Arab troops captured Damascus from the Ottoman Empire.
First World War: Germany repelled Britain's second attempt to blockade the Belgian port of Ostend.
First World War: The British Royal Navy launched unsuccessful raids on Ostend and Zeebrugge in German-occupied Belgium.
First World War: The German Army opened the Spring Offensive with Operation Michael, attempting to break through the Allied lines and to seize ports on the English Channel.
First World War: The Japanese merhant ship Hirano Maru was sunk by a German submarine in the Celtic Sea with the loss of 291 lives.
First World War: The Second Battle of Villers-Bretonneux began, which contained the first instance of tanks fighting against each other.
Forces united in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes defeated Hungarian forces to end the occupation of Međimurje.
Four days of inter-ethnic clashes broke out in Baku, Azerbaijan, resulting in about 12,000 deaths.
Giacomo Puccini's comic opera Gianni Schicchi premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in New York City.
Józef Piłsudski, appointed the commander-in-chief of Polish forces by the Regency Council, was entrusted with the creation of a national government for the newly independent Poland.
National Guards and Sokol volunteers protested in Zagreb, leading to an armed clash with regiments of the Home Guard and former Common Army.
Nestor Makhno and Fedir Shchus led insurgents to successfully ambush the Central Powers that occupied southern Ukraine during World War I.
Opha May Johnson became the first woman to enlist in the United States Marine Corps.
RMS Carpathia, which had rescued survivors of the 1912 Titanic sinking, was sunk by a German U-boat with the loss of five crew.
Russian Revolution: Tsar Nicholas II and his family were murdered by Bolsheviks at Yekaterinburg.
The Battle of Amiens began in northern France, marking the start of the Allies' Hundred Days Offensive through the German front lines that ultimately led to the end of World War I.
The Council of Lithuania signed the Act of Independence, proclaiming the restoration of an independent Lithuania.
The Podgorica Assembly convened in Montenegro, with the intention of uniting with the Kingdom of Serbia.

The Sedition Act was passed in the United States, forbidding Americans from using "disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language" about the government, flag, or armed forces during the ongoing World War I.
The United Kingdom established the Royal Air Force, near the end of the First World War.

The United States Navy suffered its largest non-combat loss of life when the collier USS Cyclops set sail from Barbados to Baltimore and was never seen again, presumably disappearing in the Bermuda Triangle.
The armistice between the German Empire and the Allies was signed in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne of France.
The government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic adopted a tricolour national flag, which is again in use today, with slight modifications, by the present-day Republic of Azerbaijan.
The short-lived Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic was established on territory formerly part of the Russian Empire.
U.S. president Woodrow Wilson announced his Fourteen Points for a moral cause and for post–World War I peace in Europe.
Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas declared the formation of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, a puppet state created by Soviet Russia to justify the Lithuanian–Soviet War.
With the signing of the Act of Union, Denmark recognized the Kingdom of Iceland as a fully sovereign state in personal union through a common monarch.
World War I: Allied forces led by the Australian general John Monash won the Battle of Hamel, demonstrating the effectiveness of combined-arms techniques in trench warfare.
World War I: An Imperial German Navy U-boat opened fire on a small convoy of barges and defending aircraft near the American town of Orleans, Massachusetts.
World War I: Armenian forces defeated Ottoman troops at the Battle of Sardarabad, halting the Turkish advance and preventing further destruction of the Armenian nation.
World War I: British and Australian troops defeated German forces at the First Battle of Dernancourt in northern France.
World War I: Italian torpedo boats sank the Austro-Hungarian dreadnought SMS Szent István off the Dalmatian coast, killing 89 of the crew.
World War I: The 26-day Battle of Belleau Wood near the Marne River in France ended with American forces finally clearing that forest of German troops.
World War I: The Battle of Nazareth ended with the British Empire victorious over the Ottomans.
World War I: The Battle of St Quentin Canal took place, which led to the British Fourth Army making the first breach of the German defensive Hindenburg Line.
World War I: The Central Powers' defeat at the Battle of Dobro Pole played a role in the Bulgarian withdrawal from the war and led to the subsequent liberation of Vardar Macedonia.
A large molasses tank in Boston, Massachusetts, burst and a wave of molasses rushed through the streets, killing 21 people and injuring 150 others.
Admiral Ludwig von Reuter scuttled the German High Seas Fleet in Scapa Flow to prevent the ships from being seized and divided amongst the Allied Powers.
After serving two years in prison for encouraging people to resist military conscription, anarchist Emma Goldman was deported from the United States to Russia.
American baseball player Babe Ruth was sold by the Boston Red Sox to their rivals, the New York Yankees, beginning the 84-year-long "Curse of the Bambino".
Bavarian socialist Kurt Eisner, who had organized the German Revolution that overthrew the Wittelsbach monarchy and established Bavaria as a republic, was assassinated.
Benito Mussolini and his supporters founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento, the predecessor of the National Fascist Party.
Communist, revolutionary-socialist, and syndicalist delegates met in Moscow to establish the Communist International.
During a general strike in Winnipeg, Canada, members of the Royal North-West Mounted Police attacked a crowd of strikers, armed with clubs and revolvers.
During the Egyptian Revolution, British authorities arrested rebel leader Saad Zaghloul and exiled him to Malta.
First Red Scare: The anarchist followers of Luigi Galleani set off eight bombs in eight cities across the United States.
Following Peace Day celebrations marking the end of the First World War, English ex-servicemen unhappy with unemployment and other grievances rioted and burned down Luton Town Hall.
Friedrich Ebert was elected the provisional president of Germany by the Weimar National Assembly.
Hundreds of Canadian soldiers rioted in Epsom, England, leading to the death of a British police officer.
Intense rioting over labour conditions broke out in Glasgow, Scotlan.
Mexican Revolution leader Emiliano Zapata was shot to death near Ciudad Ayala, Morelos.
Paris Peace Conference: Woodrow Wilson overturns Japan's Racial Equality Proposal, stating that unanimous support was required.
Polish–Soviet War: The Polish army launched the Vilna offensive to capture Vilnius (now in Lithuania) from the Red Army.
Red Summer: Race riots erupted in Chicago after a racial incident occurred on a South Side beach, leading to 38 fatalities and 537 injuries.
Russian Civil War: British motor torpedo boats raided the Bolshevik Baltic Fleet's home base of Kronstadt, sinking a depot ship and damaging a battleship.
Sir Harry Hands, the mayor of Cape Town, performed the first public observance of a two-minute silence in remembrance of those killed in World War I.
The Battle of Bereza Kartuska, the first serious armed conflict of the Polish–Soviet War, took place near present-day Biaroza, Belarus.
The Boston police strike ended after four days of rule by the state militia, the deaths of nine people, and accusations that striking officers were "agents of Lenin".
The First Dáil convened at the Mansion House in Dublin and adopted a declaration of independence calling for the establishment of the Irish Republic.
The German Workers' Party, the precursor of the Nazi Party, was founded by Anton Drexler.
The Inter-Allied Women's Conference opened as a counterpart to the Paris Peace Conference, marking the first time that women were allowed formal participation in an international treaty negotiation.
The May Fourth Movement began in China with large-scale student demonstrations in Tiananmen Square, Beijing.
The Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine defeated the White Russian Volunteer Army at the Battle of Peregonovka.
The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act was enacted, lifting most of the existing common-law restrictions on women in the United Kingdom.
The Third Anglo-Afghan War ended with the United Kingdom signing a treaty to recognise the independence of the Emirate of Afghanistan.
The U.S. Congress passed the Volstead Act over president Woodrow Wilson's veto, reinforcing Prohibition in the United States.
Ukrainian Bolsheviks led by Mykhailo Polonsky attempted to assassinate Nestor Makhno, as part of the Polonsky conspiracy.
World War I: More than 65,000 workers in Seattle began a five-day general strike to gain higher wages after two years of wage controls in the United States.
A bomb in a horse-drawn wagon exploded in front of 23 Wall Street in New York City, killing 38 people and injuring several hundred others.
A magnitude-7.9 earthquake struck Haiyuan County, China, killing more than 250,000 people.
A march by blind people from across the United Kingdom to protest poor working conditions ended at Trafalgar Square, London.
At the San Remo conference, the principal Allies of World War I passed a resolution allocating League of Nations mandates for the administration of former Ottoman territories in the Middle East.

During their national convention in Chicago, Republican Party leaders gathered in negotiations at The Blackstone Hotel to select their presidential candidate, leading to the phrase "smoke-filled room".
Franco-Syrian War: At the Battle of Maysalun, forces of the Arab Kingdom of Syria were defeated by a French army moving to occupy the territory allocated to them by the San Remo conference.
In London, the Cenotaph was unveiled and the Unknown Warrior was buried in Westminster Abbey in remembrance of the First World War.
In the United Kingdom, the Blind Persons Act received royal assent.
Irish War of Independence: British auxiliary police officers known as Black and Tans went on a rampage in Balbriggan, burning more than fifty homes and businesses and killing two people.
Irish War of Independence: Following an Irish Republican Army ambush of an Auxiliary patrol, British forces burned and looted numerous buildings in Cork.
Irish War of Independence: On Bloody Sunday in Dublin, the IRA assassinated a group of British intelligence agents, and British forces killed 14 civilians at a Gaelic football match at Croke Park.
Irish playwright and politician Terence MacSwiney died after a hunger strike in Brixton Prison, bringing the Irish struggle for independence to international attention.
Nepalese author Krishna Lal Adhikari was sentenced to nine years in prison for publishing a book about the cultivation of corn alleged to contain attacks on the ruling dynasty.
Peasants in and around Križ began a rebellion to protest economic and conscription policies enacted by the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.
Ray Chapman of the Cleveland Indians was hit by a pitch and died the following day, becoming the only Major League Baseball player to die directly as a result of injuries sustained during a game.
Russian Civil War: Peasants in Tambov Governorate began a rebellion against the Bolshevik government of Soviet Russia.
Russian Civil War: Relying on Red Army troops in neighboring Azerbaijan, the Bolsheviks attempted to stage a coup d'etat in Georgia.
The American Civil Liberties Union was founded by the directors of the National Civil Liberties Bureau.
The American Professional Football Conference, a predecessor of the National Football League, was established in Canton, Ohio.
The Battle of Radzymin, one of the bloodiest and most intense battles of the Polish–Soviet War, concluded with a Polish victory.
The Congress of Soviets approved the GOELRO plan, the first Soviet plan for national economic recovery and development.
The Grand National Assembly of Turkey, the country's unicameral legislature, first met in Ankara in the midst of the Turkish War of Independence.
The Kapp Putsch, an attempted coup aiming to undo the German Revolution of 1918–1919, briefly ousted the government of the Weimar Republic.
The Kingdom of Italy and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes signed the Treaty of Rapallo to establish national borders east of the Adriatic Sea.
The League of Nations, the first worldwide intergovernmental organization with a focus on peace and security, held its first council meeting in Paris.
The Louisiana hurricane dissipated over Kansas after forcing around 4,500 people to evacuate and causing $1.45 million in damages.
The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, guaranteeing women's suffrage in the country.
The Soviet–Lithuanian Peace Treaty was signed, with Soviet Russia agreeing to recognize an independent Lithuania.
The Svalbard Treaty was signed in Paris, recognizing Norwegian sovereignty over the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
The Volstead Act went into effect, beginning the prohibition of alcohol in the United States.
The courtesan Wang Lianying was murdered in Shanghai, leading to months of media and literary coverage.
Three African-American circus workers were lynched by a mob in Duluth, Minnesota, a crime that shocked the country for having taken place in the Northern United States.
Times Square Theater opened on Broadway with a production of The Mirage, a play written by its owner, Edgar Selwyn.

Under the leadership of Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, U.S. Department of Justice agents launched a series of raids against radical leftists and anarchists in more than 30 cities and towns across 23 states.
Adolf Hitler became leader of the National Socialist German Workers' Party.

At his trial for the assassination of Talaat Pasha, viewed as the main orchestrator of the Armenian genocide, Soghomon Tehlirian was acquitted after arguing: "I have killed a man, but I am not a murderer."
Bessie Coleman became the first Black person to earn an international pilot's license from the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale.
British Army officer Thomas Stanton Lambert was assassinated by the Irish Republican Army near Moydrum, Ireland.
Emir Abdullah established the first centralised government in the recently created British protectorate of Transjordan.
Frances Kyle was called to the Bar of Ireland, becoming the first female barrister in Ireland or Great Britain.
In Atlantic City, New Jersey, Margaret Gorman was crowned the "Golden Mermaid", the forerunner to the Miss America pageant.
Irish War of Independence: Most of the village of Knockcroghery in County Roscommon was burned by British forces.
Irish War of Independence: One day after a truce was agreed between the Irish Republican Army and British forces, violence broke out between Catholics and Protestants in Belfast.
Rioting broke out in Bombay, India, during the visit of Edward, Prince of Wales, leading to at least 58 deaths.
Russian Civil War: Bolshevik forces suppressed a rebellion of sailors and civilians in Kronstadt.
Soviet politician Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko authorised the use of chemical weapons against a peasant rebellion in the Tambov Governorate.
Talaat Pasha, the main perpetrator of the Armenian genocide, was assassinated by Soghomon Tehlirian.
The Australian Air Corps was disbanded, to be replaced the following day by the Australian Air Force.
The Australian Air Force was formed, replacing the short-lived Australian Air Corps and separating it from the Army.
The Australian cricket team, led by Warwick Armstrong, became the first team to complete a whitewash in the Ashes, an achievement that would not be repeated for 86 years.
The Bolshevik–Makhnovist conflict resumes with a surprise attack by the Red Army against the Makhnovshchina.
The Chicago Theatre, the oldest surviving grand movie palace, opened.
The Kronstadt rebellion began following mass protests in Petrograd demanding greater freedom in Russia with sailors and citizens taking up arms against the Bolsheviks.
The Mortimer War Memorial, designed by Herbert Maryon in memory of local servicemen who died in the First World War, was dedicated.
The Royal Navy's R.38, the world's largest airship at the time, was destroyed by a structural failure over Hull, killing 44 of the 49 crew aboard.

The Soviet republics of Russia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia signed the Treaty of Kars with the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, establishing the current borders between Turkey and the Caucasian states.
The first National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party opened in a house in Shanghai.
The inaugural Women's Olympiad, the first international women's sports event, opened at the International Sporting Club of Monaco in Monte Carlo.
The remains of an unknown soldier were buried with an eternal flame at the Altare della Patria in Rome.
Under the British Government of Ireland Act, Ireland was partitioned into two self-governing territories, Northern and Southern Ireland.
Workers at the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills in Madras, India, began a four-month strike.
Yan Ruisheng, the first full-length Chinese film, is released in Shanghai.
A landslide in Byblos revealed a sarcophagus in an underground tomb that was later discovered to be part of a large Bronze Age necropolis.
After nine days, the great fire of Smyrna was extinguished, having caused at least ten thousand deaths.
Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton died of a heart attack during his final expedition.
Brazilian Army rebels took over Fort Copacabana and launched a rebellion in Rio de Janeiro against President Epitácio Pessoa and President-elect Artur Bernardes.
During a general strike in Guayaquil, Ecuador, police and military fired into a crowd, killing at least 300 people.
Fountain of Time, in Chicago's Washington Park, was dedicated as a tribute to 100 years of peace between the United States and Great Britain following the Treaty of Ghent.
Gabriel Narutowicz, the first president of Poland, was assassinated only five days after having taken office.
Irish Civil War: Irish nationalist author Erskine Childers was executed by the Irish Free State for illegally carrying a semi-automatic pistol.
Irish Republican Army gunmen assassinated British member of parliament Field Marshal Sir Henry Wilson.

Irish War of Independence: In Belfast, two men wearing police uniforms broke into a house and murdered a Catholic family in what was believed to be a reprisal for the deaths of two policemen the day before.
Joseph Stalin became the first general secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
Rebecca Latimer Felton became the first woman to serve in the United States Senate, albeit for only one day.

Representatives from France, Italy, Japan, the United States, and the United Kingdom signed the Washington Naval Treaty, agreeing to limits on naval construction in the hopes of preventing an arms race.
Seven of the sixteen American railroad labor organizations staged a nationwide strike that lasted two months.
Sixteen-year-old Lilian Salkeld became the first woman to walk from London to Brighton.
The Imperial Japanese Navy commissioned Hōshō, the world's first purpose-built aircraft carrier.
The Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., featuring a sculpture of the sixteenth U.S. president Abraham Lincoln by Daniel Chester French, opened.
The Soviet government created the South Ossetian Autonomous Oblast within the Georgian SSR.
The United States Navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier, USS Langley.
The first portion of the Imperial Wireless Chain, a strategic international wireless telegraphy communications network created to link the countries of the British Empire, opened.
The largest recorded snowstorm in the history of Washington, D.C., collapsed the Knickerbocker Theatre, killing 98 people.
The tomb of Tutankhamun was discovered by a team led by British Egyptologist Howard Carter.

U.S. senator John B. Kendrick introduced a resolution calling for an investigation of a secret land deal involving U.S. president Warren G. Harding's administration, leading to the Teapot Dome scandal.
Under the South Seas Mandate, Japan set up a government in Koror, precipitating large-scale Japanese settlement in Palau.
Australian cricketer Bill Ponsford made 429 runs to break the world record for the highest first-class score.
Calvin Coolidge became the 30th president of the United States after Warren G. Harding suffered a fatal heart attack.
French drivers André Lagache and René Léonard completed the most laps during the first edition of the sports car race the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
Kitosh, an African labourer, died after having been flogged by his British employer, in a case that eventually led to reform of the legal system of the Kenya Colony.
Lithuanian residents of the Klaipėda Region began a revolt, ahead of a League of Nations decision on their future which they expected to be against their interest.
Nepal and the United Kingdom signed the first treaty that defined the international status of Nepal as an independent and a sovereign nation.
Roy and Walt Disney founded the Disney Brothers Cartoon Studio in Hollywood, which eventually grew to become one of the largest media and entertainment corporations in the world.
Stanley Bruce became prime minister of Australia as leader of the country's first Coalition government.
Ten Japanese-American children were killed in a racially motivated arson attack on a school in Sacramento, California.
The Arts Club of Chicago hosted the opening of Pablo Picasso's first solo United States showing, entitled Original Drawings by Pablo Picasso.
The FA Cup final between Bolton Wanderers and West Ham United was held on the opening day of the Empire Stadium in London.
The Gleno Dam in the Italian province of Bergamo failed due to poor workmanship, flooding the downstream valley and killing at least 356 people.
The Mandate for Palestine came into effect, officially creating the protectorates of Mandatory Palestine under British administration and Transjordan as a separate emirate under King Abdullah I.
The Treaty of Lausanne was signed to settle part of the partition of the Ottoman Empire, establishing the boundaries of Greece, Bulgaria and Turkey.
Troops from France and Belgium invaded the Ruhr to force the Weimar Republic to pay reparations in the aftermath of World War I.
A private senator's bill by Herbert Payne to introduce compulsory voting in Australia became law.
A team of U.S. Army Air Service aviators landed in Seattle, Washington, to complete the first aerial circumnavigation of the world.
Gee Jon became the first person in the United States to be executed by lethal gas.
